worksheet.title: Put It in Order
worksheet.subtitle: An algorithm is steps in the right order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can put the steps of a task in the right order.

parts.title: What is an algorithm?
parts.text: An algorithm is a set of steps you do in order to finish a job. These step-cards are mixed up. Read them, then put them in the right order so the job works. Picture doing the task to check.

parts.title: Number the steps
parts.prompt: Write 1, 2, 3, 4 on the cards above to show the right order to plant a seed. Think: what must Bit do first?

parts.title: Write the order
parts.prompt: Now write the letters in the right order in the boxes.

parts.title: You try — order it
parts.prompt: Number these cards 1 to 4 for washing hands, then write the letters in order in the boxes.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: An algorithm only works when the steps are in the right order. If two steps swap, the job can go wrong — like drying your hands before you wash them!

teacher_guide.title: Put It in Order
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 1. Put It in Order — Teacher Guide

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students read a set of mixed-up step-cards and put them in the right order to make a working algorithm, then do a second one on their own. Ordering the steps of a task is creating a sequential algorithm — a computational representation of an everyday procedure (C3.1) — and noticing that swapping steps breaks it touches C3.2.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: cut the four cards apart so students can physically slide them into order before writing.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: read the plant-a-seed cards aloud. 'What must happen first? You can't drop a seed with no hole — so dig first.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — number the cards C-A-D-B. Exercise 2 — write the letters C, A, D, B.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — wash hands in order: wet, soap, rinse, dry (B, C, D, A).
4. Connect: 'Steps in the right order make an algorithm — computers need their steps in order too.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 / Ex 2 — Plant a seed: dig a hole (C), drop the seed (A), cover the seed (D), water it (B). Order: C, A, D, B.
Ex 3 — Wash hands: wet hands (B), rub on soap (C), rinse hands (D), dry hands (A). Order: B, C, D, A.
Why the order works: each step depends on the one before — you must dig before you drop, wet before you soap. Swap two and the job fails (drying before washing leaves hands dirty).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: ordering by the card letters (A-B-C-D) instead of by the task — remind students the letters are just names, not the order.
Simplify: do the plant-a-seed task only, acting each step out together first.
Extend: ask students to name another everyday algorithm (e.g. making toast) and list its steps in order.
Success indicator: the child writes C, A, D, B and B, C, D, A and can explain why a step must come before another.
